where n is the total number of samples. It is important to note that as K increases, MAP@K may decrease due to the inclusion of less relevant images. We used the vision encoders of the supervised baseline, CT-CLIP and the fine-tuned models for volume-to-volume retrieval and assessed their performance across both internal and external validation sets using MAP@1, MAP@5, MAP@10 and MAP@50 metrics. The Recall@K metric was not applied in image-to-image retrieval due to the inherent limitation that the cosine similarity for identical images would inevitably be the highest, resulting in a consistent Recall@K value of 1. However, this issue does not arise in text-to-image retrieval since the query is based on text embeddings rather than image embeddings.

For report-to-volume retrieval, we used the pretrained text transformer and 3D vision transformer to generate vector embeddings for both radiology reports and CT volumes, which were transformed from the token space to the embedding space with the CT-CLIP’s trained projection layers (Fig. 1c). Our goal was to find the CT volume that best matched each query report. To achieve this, we computed the cosine similarity between the latent representations of each report and all the CT volumes. Subsequently, we ranked the CT volumes on the basis of their cosine similarity scores to identify and return the most relevant matches. The process of report-to-volume retrieval is depicted in Fig. 5b.

For the evaluation of this task, we employed the Recall@K metric, where K represents the number of returned images. This method serves as a standard evaluation tool in text-to-image retrieval tasks42. We assessed four Recall@K metrics: Recall@5, Recall@10, Recall@50 and Recall@100. These metrics measure the frequency of the target image appearing among the top 5, 10, 50 and 100 retrieved images, respectively. It is worth noting that the external validation set lacks text reports. Therefore, we restricted the report-to-volume retrieval evaluation to the internal validation set. We assessed both CT-CLIP and the fine-tuned model with VocabFine for this task. However, since the supervised model and ClassFine do not generate latent embeddings for reports, they were not used in the report-to-volume retrieval.

To train CT-CHAT, we curated a comprehensive VQA dataset derived from free-form reports and chest CT volumes, using the same train–validation split as CT-RATE. The dataset had four main components, with the following details for the training set.

The first component is the long-answer questions, which were further divided into four subcategories: conversation-based questions, description questions, free-response questions and text-only questions. The conversation, description and free-response questions were generated from radiology reports, while the text-only questions were created using 48,343 articles related to chest CT, retrieved from the PubMed Central–OA (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/tools/openftlist). In total, the long-answer component of the training set included 281,689 conversations, with a total of 518,053 conversation questions, 138,104 description questions, 138,061 free-response questions and 250,760 text-only questions. All questions were generated using the Llama 3.1 8B large language model43, following the methodology described in ref. 14. The scripts for generating the question–answer pairs are available in the GitHub repository, and the prompts are provided in Supplementary Table 7. The second component consists of multiple-choice questions, also generated by Llama 3.1 8B43, following the same approach described in ref. 14. This component of the training set included a total of 46,911 multiple-choice conversations, comprising 138,608 questions in total. The third component included short-answer questions derived from radiology reports in the CT-RATE dataset using a rule-based approach, as described in ref. 58. These questions covered categories such as location, presence, abnormality and disorder. A total of 1,417,828 short-answer questions were sampled to create 318,710 short-answer conversations in the training set. The fourth component involved radiology report-generation questions, totalling 47,149 conversations in the training set, where each conversation contained a single report-generation question along with the corresponding generated report. The report-generation questions were randomly selected from a predefined set of questions (Supplementary Table 6).

The validation set was curated similarly to the training set, using the free-form reports from the CT-RATE validation set. The validation dataset included 33,326 conversation questions, 8,886 description questions, 8,888 free-response questions, 12,013 short-answer questions, 8,915 multiple-choice questions and 3,039 report-generation questions. Extended Data Fig. 7 shows example entries from the described dataset. Since the VQA dataset was generated by a large language model, we carefully selected only accurately generated and properly formatted data, that is, data that could be successfully parsed as JavaScript Object Notation for training our models. In addition, we limited the initial number of generated questions to maintain a reasonable training duration. Our VQA dataset has been made publicly available alongside CT-RATE.

Adapted from the LLaVa framework59, CT-CHAT integrates the frozen CT-CLIP vision encoder, a multimodal projector module and a large language model to enhance multimodal processing capabilities. The visual encoder compresses 3D chest CT volumes into a low-dimensional feature space. The multimodal projector module then transforms these visual features into the LLM’s embedding space, aligning it with text tokens. The LLM processes these visual–language tokens as input to generate contextual responses. Figure 6a summarizes the architecture of the CT-CHAT model.

In our implementation, we evaluated and compared four different LLMs. For the primary configuration of CT-CHAT, we used the 70B Meta Llama (3.1)43, one of the state-of-the-art open-source LLMs. This model consists of 80 transformer layers, 64 attention heads, an embedding dimension of 8,192 and a feed-forward network (FFN) dimension of 28,672, and supports a context size of up to 128,000 tokens. For a smaller model, we used the 8B Meta Llama (3.1)43, which includes 32 transformer layers, 32 attention heads, an embedding dimension of 4,096, an FFN dimension of 14,336 and a context size of up to 128,000 tokens. In addition, for comparison, we implemented two LLMs used in the official LLaVA (1.6)26: Vicuna 13B and Mistral 7B. Figure 6d shows the scores for each of these LLMs. To dynamically adjust the model’s output mode on the basis of the specific task, we added four special tokens to the tokenizers of each model: <long_answer>, <short_answer>, <report_generation> and <multiple_choice>. These tokens were selected for different tasks during training and inference. The multimodal projector, based on the approach described in ref. 14, consists of an attention-pooling layer, followed by a 2-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP). The attention-pooling mechanism uses 256 learned latent queries in conjunction with multiheaded cross-attention to compress the final layer’s features from the encoder backbone into a fixed-length sequence of image tokens. This approach optimizes both training and inference, ensuring that the sequence length remains within the LLM’s context window and making the model focus more on the important features with the attention mechanism. The MLP that follows was adapted from LLava (1.6)26 and includes a single hidden layer activated by GeLU, transforming the image tokens to match the LLM’s embedding dimension.

Training CT-CHAT involved two steps. First, in the medical concept alignment step, the LLM was frozen, and the multimodal projector was trained with the input ‘Please provide the radiology report for the following chest CT volume <image>’ and the output report. This step improves subsequent fine-tuning performance and helps the multimodal projector to be aligned in biomedical concepts27. We conducted an ablation study of this step to show its effect (Supplementary Table 10b). In the second step, medical instruction tuning, the model was trained with the CT-VQA dataset that includes long-answer, short-answer, multiple-choice and report-generation question–answer pairs. During this step, the multimodal projector, along with LORA weights44 for the LLM with rank 128 and alpha 256, was fine-tuned. <image> tokens were added to indicate the embedded image input to the model, except for text-only questions and answers. The four special tokens were added to the respective question–answer pairs in the dataset, enabling the model to learn different output modes. These tokens were later used during inference to select different modes of the model. The hyperparameters for each model for pretraining and fine-tuning are provided in Supplementary Table 4a,b. To boost report-generation accuracy, we fine-tuned CT-CHAT with structured metadata extracted exclusively from pulmonary-nodule masks. Each CT-RATE volume was processed with TotalSegmentator60, from which we recorded, per nodule, the lobar location, centroid, orthogonal diameters and volume (mm3). These fields were embedded in a fixed prompt:
<volume_tokens>
Generate a detailed radiology report for the given chest CT volume.
<BEGIN_NODULE_INFO>
Nodule_Count: n
Nodule_ID: 1 7D2Lobe: left lower
Centroid_mm: (x,y,z)
Diameter_mm: (x: dx, y: dy, z: dz)
Volume_mm3: v
… (repeat for each nodule)
<END_NODULE_INFO>

Each sample included (1) CT volume features from the frozen CT-CLIP encoder, (2) the structured nodule template and (3) the reference report. Fine-tuning was performed on the 8B Llama 3.1 configuration of CT-CHAT using LoRA (rank 128, α = 256); only the LoRA weights and projector were updated. Supplying these segmentation-derived cues markedly improved performance (Fig. 6e). The same workflow could incorporate additional abnormalities as more 3D segmentation models become available.

Given the lack of pretrained VQA models for 3D imaging, we conducted a comparative analysis of CT-CHAT against four 2D state-of-the-art open-source VQA models: LLaVA 1.6 (Mistral 7B)26, LLaVA 1.6 (Vicuna 13B)26, LLaVA-Med27 and CXR-LLaVA28, using the benchmarking framework established in ref. 14. To address the challenge of representing 3D information using their 2D encoders and to ensure a fair comparison, we used DRRs derived from CT-RATE, as suggested by ref. 45. This approach was chosen over the selection of random or central CT slices, which could not adequately capture all relevant pathologies. The use of DRRs was justified, as ref. 45 demonstrates that models trained with DRRs show comparable results to those trained with 3D chest CTs.

To evaluate the baseline models and CT-CHAT models with different LLMs, we employed four NLP metrics: BLEU-1 (ref. 61), METEOR62, ROUGE-L63 and CIDEr64, along with the Llama score, which measures the clinical accuracy of the generated responses compared to the ground truth, using the Llama 3.1 70B model43. A similar LLM-based clinical accuracy measurement approach was used in Llava-Med with the GPT-4 API27. Supplementary Table 8 presents the system prompt for the Llama 3.1 model, which was used to score the generated answers. We calculated scores specifically for each task: long answer, short answer, multiple choice and report generation. Figure 6c illustrates mean and task-specific scores for each model. To visualize the clinical accuracy of the models, we categorized the Llama scores for every question in each task into three ranges: 0–3 for low clinical accuracy, 4–6 for average clinical accuracy and 7–10 for high clinical accuracy, and created Sankey plots within these ranges (Supplementary Fig. 10).

In addition to benchmarking CT-CHAT on VQA tasks, we further evaluated its performance in radiology report generation, a task more reflective of routine radiological workflows, by comparing it with two state-of-the-art 3D report-generation models: RadFM29 and CT2Rep30. While VQA metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE and the Llama score assess linguistic and clinical quality, they do not fully capture diagnostic use. Therefore, for this comparison we employed clinical-efficacy metrics: precision, recall, F1 and the CRG score65. CRG weights findings by prevalence and severity, giving a distribution-aware score aligned with radiologists’ priorities. Metric computation used our automated report labeller, which extracts structured abnormality labels from the generated reports. Evaluation was conducted on both the internal CT-RATE validation set and the external RAD-ChestCT dataset; for RAD-ChestCT, which lacks text reports, we leveraged its binary abnormality annotations to enable indirect evaluation through our labeller. Notably, we used the original pretrained weights for both RadFM and CT2Rep without retraining.

To complement automatic metrics, we performed a blinded, three-reader study of report quality. Two board-certified thoracic radiologists from Zurich (R1, R2) and one from Istanbul (R3) independently rated reports generated by CT-CHAT, RadFM and CT2Rep. Because free-text scoring is time-intensive, we limited the pool to 150 CT-RATE validation cases per model. Cases were stratified rather than randomly sampled: after computing Llama scores for CT-CHAT outputs, we selected 50 volumes from each accuracy band (low 0–3, medium 4–6, high 7–10) to ensure balanced difficulty. For every selected scan, the three anonymized model outputs were presented, and readers scored each report on a 0–10 scale against predefined criteria covering finding description, localization, terminology and overall clinical adequacy. Figure 6d shows the results: CT-CHAT achieved mean scores of 3.44 (R1), 4.10 (R2) and 4.52 (R3), outperforming RadFM (0.55, 0.91, 0.86) and CT2Rep (2.66, 2.52, 2.74). Violin plots display a right-shifted distribution for CT-CHAT, confirming superior perceived clinical fidelity. The same protocol can be repeated for larger or external cohorts as new models emerge. It is important to note CT-CHAT’s superiority over CT2Rep, even though both models were trained on the same CT-RATE dataset. Moreover, CT2Rep is optimized solely for report generation, while CT-CHAT is tuned primarily for VQA tasks, classification and question answering, and only secondarily for report generation. Despite this, CT-CHAT consistently outperformed CT2Rep across all evaluations. The performance gap underscores the value of contrastive pretraining with CT-CLIP in capturing clinically meaningful 3D CT representations that transfer effectively to downstream tasks, even when the model is not explicitly trained for them.

To evaluate CT-CHAT’s ability to retrieve information from chest CT, we conducted an ablation study for the image provision, as shown in Supplementary Table 10a. Since the model is expected to hallucinate pathologies when the input volume is not provided, we implemented a guardrail for prevention with the system prompt in Supplementary Table 9. Supplementary Fig. 11 provides an example of the guardrail.

Experiments for CT-CLIP were conducted using Python 3.11.5 with PyTorch 2.0.1, CUDA 11.7 and other libraries such as SciPy 1.11.1, Torchvision 0.15.2, Scikit-learn 1.3.0, Pandas 2.0.3, NumPy 1.24.4, Transformers 4.30.1 and Accelerate 0.21.1. For CT-CHAT, Python 3.12.4 was used with PyTorch v.2.4.0, CUDA v.12.4, SciPy v.14.0, Torchvision v.0.19.0, Scikit-learn v.1.2.2, Pandas v.2.2.2 and NumPy v.1.26.4. Fine-tuning of CT-CLIP and other experiments was performed on a single A100 GPU.
